ta-l1d1q2-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph setting the agenda of Question 2. Having treated the acts of enjoyment and use, Thomas turns to their objects, first what is to be enjoyed and then what is to be used. On the first he poses two articles: whether God alone is to be enjoyed, and whether he is enjoyed by one enjoyment or by several.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3510.summary: First objection. According to Lombard's text, we are to enjoy the things that make us blessed. Created beatitude makes us blessed, so it too is to be enjoyed, and not God alone.
claims: Whatever makes us blessed is to be enjoyed, and created beatitude makes us blessed.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3513.summary: Second objection. A human being's ultimate end is their happiness, which is their most perfect operation, and we are to enjoy the ultimate end. So we are to enjoy that operation. This is supported by Aristotle (happiness is not sought for anything else) and Boethius (beatitude is a state made perfect by the aggregation of all goods).
claims: Happiness, the most perfect operation, is the ultimate human end and so an object of enjoyment.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3519.summary: Third objection, from Cicero's definition of the honestum as what draws us by its own power and attracts us by its dignity. What attracts of itself is loved for its own sake, so every honestum, and therefore every virtue, is to be enjoyed.
claims: The honestum draws us by its own dignity and so is loved for its own sake.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3526.summary: Fourth objection, from Philemon 20 ('I will enjoy you in the Lord'). We can enjoy a just person, and so, it seems, any human being as bearing God's image, and any creature as bearing his vestige.
claims: Paul speaks of enjoying a fellow human being in the Lord.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3537.summary: Sed contra. Goodness is the ground of love, and all goodness is referred to God's goodness, from which it flows and whose likeness it bears. So nothing is to be loved except in ordering to God, and God alone is to be enjoyed.
claims: All created goodness flows from and resembles divine goodness and is therefore to be loved in ordering to God.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3540.summary: Second sed contra, from Proverbs 16:4: God made all things for himself. He is therefore the end of all things, and everything is to be loved for his sake.
claims: God is the end of all things, since he made all things for himself.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3551.summary: Thomas's determination distinguishes three senses of enjoying something. (1) As object: in this sense God alone is to be enjoyed, because the whole goodness of the universe is ordered to his goodness, as the good of an army is ordered to its leader (Metaphysics 12). (2) As the habit eliciting the act of enjoyment: in this sense we enjoy created beatitude and charity. (3) As the instrument of enjoyment: in this sense we enjoy the power whose act enjoyment is.
claims: God alone is to be enjoyed as object.
Created beatitude and charity are enjoyed as the habit eliciting enjoyment, and the power as its instrument.
The whole goodness of the universe is ordered to divine goodness as an army's good is ordered to its leader.
concepts: object, habit, and instrument of enjoyment

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3554.summary: Reply to the first objection. Something makes us blessed in two ways: effectively, as God does, and in this sense he alone is enjoyed as object; or formally, as whiteness makes a thing white, and in this sense created beatitude makes us blessed and is 'enjoyed' formally speaking.
claims: God makes us blessed effectively; created beatitude makes us blessed formally.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3557.summary: Reply to the second objection. The object of an operation terminates and perfects it and is its end, so no operation can have the character of ultimate end. But because we attain the object only through the operation, the desire for the operation and for the object is one. If we in some way enjoy enjoyment itself, it is insofar as it joins us to God. We enjoy the end and the operation by the same enjoyment, as by the same act I understand an intelligible and understand that I understand.
claims: No operation can be the ultimate end, since its object terminates and perfects it.
We enjoy the end and the operation by one and the same act, just as an act of understanding includes awareness of itself.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3561.summary: Reply to the third objection, distinguishing two senses of 'for its own sake'. As opposed to 'for the sake of another', virtues and the honestum are not loved for their own sake, since they are referred to something further. As opposed to 'accidentally', they are loved for their own sake, since they have something in their nature that moves us to love them, even if nothing else came of them; and something can be loved for itself and still be ordered to another (Ethics 1). By contrast, a bitter potion is desired only as producing health and is in no way loved for itself. 'For its own sake' may thus name a formal cause, as with virtue, or a final cause, as with God.
claims: Virtues are loved for their own sake as opposed to accidentally, but not as opposed to being referred to another.
Something may be loved for itself and yet be ordered to a further end.
concepts: formal vs. final cause of love

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3564.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. A just person is not to be enjoyed simply but in God: God is the object of enjoyment, and the holy person represents him through the likeness of grace in which God dwells. It does not follow that sinners are to be enjoyed in God, since they lack the grace that makes God indwell and that expresses the highest goodness. Still less does it follow for irrational creatures, since the likeness of image and vestige is insufficient; the likeness of grace is required.
claims: A just person may be enjoyed only in God, through the likeness of grace in which God dwells.
The likeness of image or vestige does not suffice for enjoying a creature in God; the likeness of grace is required.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3576.summary: First objection against a single enjoyment. Acts are distinguished by their objects, and the objects of enjoyment are three things distinguished by personal properties: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. So there are three enjoyments.
claims: Acts are distinguished according to their objects.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3579.summary: Second objection. An operation that stops at the common is not perfect until it reaches what is proper, as knowledge of a genus is perfected by knowledge of the difference, and desire and love even more so. Since enjoyment is a perfect operation, we will enjoy not only the essence common to the three persons but each person and its properties, so enjoyment is not one.
claims: Cognitive and appetitive operations are perfected only when they reach what is proper and particular.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3582.summary: Third objection. The Son is accustomed to refer what he has to the Father (John 7:16), and he receives goodness from the Father by birth, as he receives essence. So enjoyment of the Son's goodness should be referred to enjoyment of the Father, and the persons are not enjoyed equally, still less by one enjoyment.
claims: The Son receives goodness from the Father as he receives essence.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3592.summary: Sed contra. Just as the Trinity is one principle of all things, it is one end of all things. The operation of the Trinity as one principle is one and common, so the enjoyment of the three as one end is one.
claims: The Trinity is one principle and one end of all things.
concepts: Trinity as one principle and end

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3595.summary: Second sed contra. According to the Philosopher, the operation of happiness concerns the noblest object, and what is said by way of superabundance belongs to only one thing. So enjoyment, the operation of ultimate happiness, regards one object, and we enjoy the three persons insofar as they are one.
claims: The operation of happiness is directed to the single noblest object.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3598.summary: Thomas's determination: we enjoy the three persons by one enjoyment, for two reasons. On the side of the essence, the object of enjoyment is the highest goodness, which is numerically one in the three, so the enjoyment is one. On the side of the properties, whoever knows one relative knows its correlative, and since enjoyment arises from vision, whoever enjoys one relative as such also enjoys the other. The persons are distinguished only by relations, so enjoyment of one includes enjoyment of the others. The first reason is better, since it concerns the formal character of the object, from which an act has its unity.
claims: The three persons are enjoyed by one enjoyment because the highest goodness, the formal object of enjoyment, is numerically one in them.
Since the persons are distinguished only by relations, enjoying one includes enjoying the others.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3601.summary: Reply to the first objection. The three persons are not distinguished in what makes them objects of enjoyment; in that respect, the highest goodness, they are united.
claims: The persons are united, not distinguished, in the formal character by which they are enjoyed.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3604.summary: Reply to the second objection. We do enjoy each person's property, such as paternity, but paternity is not the formal ground of enjoyment. We enjoy it insofar as it is really the same as the highest goodness, though differing in concept.
claims: Personal properties are enjoyed insofar as they are really identical with the highest goodness while differing from it in concept.

ta-l1d1q2-d1e3607.summary: Reply to the third objection. Referring the Son's goodness to the Father implies only an order of nature, not a degree of goodness in Father and Son, so the equality and unity of enjoyment remain.
claims: Reference of the Son to the Father implies an order of nature, not inequality of goodness.

ta-l1d1q2-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 turns from the acts of enjoyment and use to their objects, beginning with what is to be enjoyed. It announces two articles: whether God alone is to be enjoyed, and whether the enjoyment is one or many.

ta-l1d1q2-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks whether God alone is to be enjoyed. Objections propose created beatitude, happiness as the most perfect operation, the virtues as honestum, and just persons (Philemon 20) as further objects of enjoyment. Against them, all created goodness is referred to God's goodness, and God made all things for himself. Thomas distinguishes enjoying something as object, as eliciting habit, and as instrument: God alone is enjoyed as object, while created beatitude, charity, and the power are 'enjoyed' only in the latter senses. The replies distinguish effective from formal beatification and explain that no operation can be the ultimate end, though end and operation are enjoyed in one act. They separate two senses of 'for its own sake', so that virtues are loved for themselves without being ultimate ends. And they allow just persons to be enjoyed only 'in God', through the likeness of grace, which sinners and irrational creatures lack.
claims: God alone is to be enjoyed as object; created beatitude and charity are enjoyed only as habit or form.
No operation can be the ultimate end.
Creatures may be enjoyed only in God, by the likeness of grace.

ta-l1d1q2-Dd1e3568.summary: Article 2 asks whether the three divine persons are enjoyed by one enjoyment or by several. Objections argue from the distinction of acts by objects, from the need for perfect operations to reach what is proper, and from the Son's reference of his goodness to the Father. The sed contra appeals to the Trinity as one principle and one end and to the unicity of the noblest object. Thomas holds that enjoyment is one, chiefly because its formal object, the highest goodness, is numerically one in the three persons, and secondarily because relatives are known and enjoyed together. Personal properties such as paternity are enjoyed insofar as they are really identical with the highest goodness, and the Son's reference to the Father implies an order of nature, not inequality.
claims: The three persons are enjoyed by a single enjoyment, whose formal object is the one highest goodness.
Personal properties are enjoyed as really identical with the divine goodness.

ta-l1d1q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 1 treats the object of enjoyment. Article 1 holds that God alone is to be enjoyed as object, because all created goodness is ordered to his goodness. It distinguishes the object of enjoyment from the habit (created beatitude, charity) and power through which we enjoy, and it allows creatures, such as just persons, to be enjoyed only in God through the likeness of grace. Article 2 holds that the three persons are enjoyed by one enjoyment, since its formal object, the highest goodness, is numerically one in them. Personal properties are enjoyed insofar as they are really identical with that goodness. Both articles rest on the principle that the unity and ordering of an act follow from the formal character of its object.
claims: God alone is the object of enjoyment; created beatitude and charity are enjoyed only formally or as habit.
The Trinity is enjoyed by a single enjoyment because divine goodness is numerically one.
